title: Largest Value Inside Exactly One Window
statement:
You get an integer array nums and an integer k. Look at all n − k + 1 contiguous windows of length k.

A value is nearly absent if exactly one of those windows contains it (anywhere, any number of times). Return the largest nearly absent value, or -1 if there is none.

examples.why: The windows are [4, 9, 2], [9, 2, 9] and [2, 9, 7]. 9 is the biggest value but sits in all three. Only 4 and 7 are inside a single window, and 7 is larger.
Each 5 is inside only one window, but the two copies are in different windows, so the value 5 appears in two windows. 1 is in both.
With k = 1 each window is one element. 3 shows up in two windows, 8 in one.

hints: Brute force is fine at this size: for each value, count the windows that contain it. But think about which positions are covered by only one window.
If 1 < k < n, every position except the first and the last is covered by at least two windows. So only nums[0] and nums[n − 1] can be candidates, and only if their value appears nowhere else.
Handle the two special cases first: k = n (one window: return the maximum) and k = 1 (each element is a window: return the largest value that occurs once).

explain.intuition:
Count how many windows cover each position. Position i is covered by windows starting from max(0, i − k + 1) to min(i, n − k). When 1 < k < n, only the very first and very last positions are covered by exactly one window; everything in between is covered by two or more. So a value can be nearly absent only if it sits at one of the two ends and nowhere else in the array.

The two edges of the range behave differently. With k = n there is one window covering everything, so the answer is the maximum. With k = 1 every element is its own window, so the answer is the largest value that occurs exactly once. Spotting these cases is the whole problem; the brute force that counts windows per value is a good way to confirm them.
steps: If k == 1, count every value and return the largest one with count 1, or -1.
Otherwise, nums[0] is a candidate if it does not occur anywhere else in the array; the same for nums[n − 1].
Return the larger valid candidate, or -1 if neither is valid.
pitfalls: Checking only that an end value appears once in its own window. In [5, 1, 5] with k = 2, each 5 is in one window but the value is in two.
Treating the first and last element as independent when they are equal. In [3, 1, 2, 3] the 3 at each end disqualifies the other.
Forgetting the special cases. With k = 1 any element can qualify, not just the ends.

complexity.space: O(n) for the counts when k = 1

solutions.title: Count windows per value
solutions.idea: For each distinct value, scan every window and count how many contain it. Keep the largest value with count 1.

solutions.title: Only the ends can qualify
solutions.idea: For 1 < k < n only the first and last positions are in a single window, so check those two values. Handle k = n and k = 1 separately.

followups: Instead of the largest value, return how many values are in exactly one window.
Generalise: return the largest value contained in exactly m windows. Does a per-value union of covered window ranges still work in O(n)?
lcTitle: Find the Largest Almost Missing Integer
